children.title: Optical Instruments
children.summary: One lens can only do so much. Stack a second one behind it in just the right place and you've built a microscope, a telescope, or a camera — the same ray diagrams, wired in series.
children.content:
# Optical Instruments ## The Idea A single lens can only do so much. Your eye already has one, and it can't zoom in on a distant galaxy or reveal a bacterium — for those, you need to stack multiple lenses (or lenses and mirrors) so that one does the initial work and a second one takes what the first produced and pushes it further. Cameras, microscopes, and telescopes are really just different combinations of the same converging-lens ray diagrams you've already learned, wired together in series. ## The Camera: One Lens, Just Like Your Eye A basic camera is the simplest instrument of the three: a single converging lens forms a real, inverted, reduced image directly onto a sensor (or old-fashioned film), exactly the way your eye's lens focuses onto the retina. Auto-focus just moves the lens back and forth to keep that real image landing precisely on the sensor as the distance to the subject changes — the camera equivalent of your eye's accommodation. ## The Microscope: Magnifying What's Tiny and Close A compound **microscope** uses two converging lenses to magnify something small that's very close to the lens: 1. The **objective lens** (short focal length, closest to the specimen) forms a real, enlarged image of the tiny object. 2. The **eyepiece lens** then acts as a simple magnifying glass on *that* image — the object sits inside the eyepiece's focal point, so the final image is virtual, upright relative to the first image, and magnified again. The two magnifications multiply together, which is how a microscope reaches magnifications a single lens never could on its own. ## The Telescope: Gathering Light from Far Away A refracting **telescope** also uses two converging lenses, but solves a different problem — the object isn't tiny, it's just extremely far away, so almost no light from it reaches your eye directly. 1. The **objective lens** is large in diameter and has a long focal length. Its main job is collecting as much light as possible from a faint, distant source and forming a small real image at its focal point. 2. The **eyepiece lens** has a short focal length and is positioned so that the real image falls right at (or near) its own focal point — it then works like a magnifying glass, sending that image to your eye as a magnified virtual image.
The objective forms a small real image; the eyepiece then magnifies it like a magnifying glass.
## Reflecting Telescopes: Swap the Lens for a Mirror Big glass lenses are heavy, expensive to cast without flaws, and bend different colours of light by slightly different amounts (an issue called chromatic aberration, which you'll meet again in the next lesson). A **reflecting telescope** solves this by using a large concave mirror instead of an objective lens to gather and focus the light — mirrors don't have that colour-bending problem, and a mirror only needs support on its back, so it can be built far larger than a lens of the same size ever could. Almost every major research telescope built today, including space telescopes, is a reflector for exactly this reason. ## Comparing the Three | Instrument | Main job | Setup | |---|---|---| | Camera | Record an image | One converging lens → real image on a sensor | | Microscope | Magnify something tiny and close | Two converging lenses, both short focal length | | Telescope | Magnify something distant and gather faint light | Large-diameter objective (long f) + small eyepiece (short f) | ## Common Mistakes - Thinking a telescope's most important number is magnification. Its real superpower is **light-gathering** — a bigger objective (lens or mirror) collects more light from faint, distant objects, which is why professional telescopes are built enormous. - Mixing up microscope and telescope objectives: a microscope's objective has a *short* focal length and sits close to a tiny object; a telescope's objective has a *long* focal length and is built wide to catch light from something impossibly far away. - Assuming only lenses can form images in an optical instrument — curved mirrors follow the exact same real/virtual image rules and are just as valid a building block. ## Quick Gut-Check Professional astronomers almost always use reflecting telescopes with mirrors rather than refracting telescopes with lenses for their biggest instruments. Based on what you now know about the size and weight limits of glass lenses, why do you think that is?

children.title: Light and Colour
children.summary: A red apple isn't red in the dark. Colour isn't something an object owns — it's what's left over after the object absorbs everything else and reflects the rest back to your eye.
children.content:
# Light and Colour ## The Idea A red apple isn't "red" in the dark — turn off every light in the room and it's just as colourless as everything else. Colour isn't a property an object owns; it's a conversation between the light hitting an object and what that object does to it. Once you know that white light is a mix of every visible wavelength (from the first lesson in this unit), the whole story of why anything looks any colour at all comes down to just three words: absorb, reflect, transmit. ## Absorption, Reflection, and Transmission When light hits a material, each wavelength gets one of three fates: - **Absorbed** — the material takes in that wavelength's energy (often converting it to heat) and it never leaves. - **Reflected** — that wavelength bounces back off the surface, which is what reaches your eye and registers as colour. - **Transmitted** — that wavelength passes through the material, which only happens with transparent or translucent materials. A **red apple** looks red because its skin absorbs every visible wavelength *except* red, which it reflects back to your eye. A pane of **blue glass** looks blue because it transmits blue wavelengths through to the other side while absorbing (and partly reflecting) the rest. A **white** surface reflects nearly all wavelengths equally; a **black** surface absorbs nearly all of them, which is exactly why black clothing feels hotter in direct sunlight — there's more absorbed energy with nowhere else to go. | Object appears... | What it does to visible light | |---|---| | White | Reflects almost all wavelengths | | Black | Absorbs almost all wavelengths | | Red | Reflects red, absorbs the rest | | Transparent/clear | Transmits nearly all wavelengths | | Green (a leaf) | Reflects green (chlorophyll absorbs red and blue for photosynthesis) | ## Additive Colour Mixing: Combining Light When you combine coloured *light*, you're adding wavelengths together, and more wavelengths present means the result gets closer to white. The three **additive primary colours** — red, green, and blue (RGB) — are the set every phone, TV, and computer screen is built from: each pixel is really three tiny lights mixing at a distance. ``` Red light + Green light = Yellow Green light + Blue light = Cyan Red light + Blue light = Magenta Red + Green + Blue = White ```
Adding coloured light moves toward white — the opposite of mixing paint.
## Subtractive Colour Mixing: Combining Pigments Paints, inks, and dyes work the opposite way. A pigment doesn't add wavelengths — it **absorbs** (subtracts) some wavelengths from the white light hitting it and reflects the rest. Mixing pigments together means each one is removing its own share of wavelengths, so the more colours you combine, the *less* light survives to reach your eye — which is why mixing lots of paint colours together tends toward muddy brown or black, never white. Printers use **cyan, magenta, and yellow (CMY)** as subtractive primaries for exactly this reason, adding black ink (K) separately because CMY alone rarely makes a true, deep black. | | Additive (light) | Subtractive (pigment) | |---|---|---| | Primaries | Red, Green, Blue | Cyan, Magenta, Yellow | | Combining more colours moves toward... | White | Black | | Starting point | Darkness (no light) | White light source, reflected off pigment | | Real-world example | Screens, stage lighting | Paint, ink, printing | ## Common Mistakes - Saying an object "is" a colour, full stop — an apple only looks red *under white light*; light it with pure blue light and it looks nearly black, because there's no red wavelength present for it to reflect. - Mixing up additive and subtractive rules — remember light *adds toward white*, pigment *subtracts toward black*. Mixing red and green **light** gives yellow; mixing red and green **paint** gives a muddy brown, not yellow. - Assuming a black object absorbs light and that's the end of the story — that absorbed energy doesn't vanish, it converts to heat, which is exactly why dark surfaces heat up faster in sunlight. ## Quick Gut-Check If you shine only pure red light and pure blue light onto a white wall so their circles overlap, what colour would you expect to see in the overlapping region — and what colour would that same overlap be if you were mixing red and blue paint instead?
